b.v: About 25 minutes. Everything here runs in your browser already - JavaScript is the one language every browser speaks.
1) console.log
This is how JavaScript shows you something. Press Run.
Change the name and run it again. The box is yours - break it, fix it, that is what it is for.
2) Storing a value
let makes a variable. No type to declare - JavaScript works it out from what you put in.
3) let against const
let can be changed later. const cannot. Try it:
TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. JavaScript refuses.

Use const by default and let only when you know the value must change. It is not fussiness - it means a wrong reassignment is caught by the machine instead of by you, later, in something that matters.
You will see var in older code and older tutorials. It behaves oddly in ways that caused real bugs for years. Do not use it. let and const replaced it and there is no reason to go back.
4) Semicolons
JavaScript usually works out where a line ends without one. Usually. There are cases where it guesses wrong, and they are unpleasant to debug. Put them in and stop thinking about it.
5) Your first error
ReferenceError: tow is not defined. JavaScript has never heard of tow. Note that one printed and three did not - it stops where the error is.
6) Comments

day-2.t: Day 2 - Numbers, text and the traps

b.v: Today's goal

v: Do arithmetic
Join text together
Understand why == is dangerous

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) Arithmetic
% gives the remainder. n % 2 is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd, which is how you test for even.
JavaScript has one kind of number, and division never gives a whole number automatically. 10 / 3 is 3.333..., and 9 / 3 is 3. If you need a whole number use Math.floor().
2) Text
3) Template strings
Backticks, not quotes. Anything inside ${} gets worked out and dropped in. Use these instead of joining with plus - they are easier to read and harder to get wrong.
The backtick is usually the key left of 1, above Tab.
4) The plus sign has two jobs

"5" + 3 gives "53", because with text involved plus means join. But "5" - 3 gives 2, because minus has no other meaning so JavaScript converts the text to a number. This inconsistency is real, it is famous, and it causes bugs. When a number arrives as text, convert it yourself with Number().
5) == against ===
Two equals converts before comparing, so a number can equal a string. Three equals does not convert - different types are simply not equal.
Always use ===. The conversions == performs are surprising enough that experienced programmers get them wrong. There is no case in normal code where you need ==.
6) Useful string methods

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) if and else
Round brackets hold the question, curly brackets hold what to do. Change 20 to 15 and run it again.
If you did the Python course: the idea is identical, but Python used a colon and indentation where JavaScript uses brackets. Indentation here is only for humans - the machine ignores it.
2) More paths
Order matters. Put 60 first and everything above 60 would get a C, because JavaScript stops at the first true one.
3) and, or, not

v: && = and, both must be true
|| = or, one is enough
! = not, flips it

b.v: 4) What counts as false
Look at the last two. The text "0" is true because it is not empty. And an empty array is true as well, which surprises everybody. Only six things are false: false, 0, "", null, undefined and NaN.
5) A shortcut worth knowing
|| falls back when the left side is falsy - but 0 is falsy, so it replaces a real zero, which is usually wrong. ?? only falls back on null or undefined, which is nearly always what you meant.
6) The short form
Question mark then colon: if this, use that, otherwise the other. Good for one small choice, bad for anything longer - reach for if instead.

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) An array

Counting starts at zero, so the third item is [2]. Ask for fruits[5] and you get undefined rather than an error - JavaScript will not stop you, which makes this mistake quieter and harder to find than in most languages.
2) Adding and removing
const on an array stops you replacing the whole array, but not changing what is inside it. push still works. That surprises people - const is about the name, not the contents.
3) Looping
for...of walks the values directly. Cleaner than counting with an index, and harder to get wrong.
4) The three methods you will use daily

v: map = same number of items, each one changed
filter = fewer items, the ones that pass
reduce = one value out of many

b.v: n => n * 2 is an arrow function - a small function written inline. Read it as: given n, give back n times two. These three methods are everywhere in real JavaScript, so it is worth running this box a few times with different numbers.
5) Finding things
6) Sorting, and a trap
Plain sort() turns everything into text first, so 100 comes before 9 because "1" is before "9". For numbers you must pass (a, b) => a - b. This has bitten more people than any other array behaviour.
The [...nums] makes a copy, because sort changes the original array rather than returning a new one.

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) An object
An array holds things in order. An object holds them by name - which is what you want for a person, a product, a setting.
Dot notation reads better. The square brackets are for when the key is in a variable.
2) Changing and adding
3) A name that is not there

Asking for a missing key gives undefined quietly. Trying to use it then fails with: Cannot read properties of undefined. That second message is one of the most common errors in all of JavaScript, and it always means the same thing - something was not there and you used it anyway.
The ?. is a question mark before the dot. It means: if this is missing, stop and give undefined rather than throwing. It saves a great deal of defensive code.
4) Objects inside objects
5) An array of objects
This is how real data almost always arrives - rows of records.
6) Pulling values out
This is destructuring. It takes the named parts out into their own variables. You will see it constantly in React, so it is worth getting used to now.

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) The ordinary way
2) return against console.log

console.log shows something on screen. return hands it back to whoever called. A function that only logs gives back undefined, and you cannot do arithmetic with undefined. This catches people for weeks.
3) Arrow functions
When the body is a single expression you can drop the brackets and the word return - the value falls out on its own. That is why n => n * 2 works.
4) Functions passed to other functions
This is the part that makes JavaScript feel different. A function is a value - you can hand it to something else.
twice takes a function and a value, and applies the function twice. That idea - passing behaviour around - is behind map, filter, event handlers and most of React.
5) Defaults
6) Where names live
The total inside belongs to the function. Setting it does not touch the one outside. That is deliberate - a function should not quietly reach out and change its surroundings.

b.v: Today's goal

v: Read an error properly
Catch one instead of crashing
Know the three you will meet most

b.v: About 25 minutes.
1) The three common ones

js
console.log(missingThing);

v: ReferenceError = a name JavaScript has never seen
Cannot read properties of undefined = something was missing and you used it anyway
is not a function = you called something that is not one

b.v: The second is the most common error in JavaScript by a wide margin. It nearly always means a value further back was undefined - so look at where that thing came from, not at the line that failed.
2) Catching
Without the try, the program stops there. With it, the catch runs and the rest carries on.
3) Where it belongs

Not everything needs a try. Number() does not throw - it gives NaN, so a check is simpler and clearer. Use try for things that genuinely throw: JSON.parse, network calls, anything outside your control.
Never write catch (e) {} with nothing inside. It swallows the error and leaves you with a program that misbehaves silently. At minimum, log it.
4) Throwing your own
Throwing on bad input is better than returning something wrong. A wrong answer travels quietly through a program; an error stops where the problem is.
5) NaN, the odd one
NaN does not equal itself, so you cannot test for it with ===. Use Number.isNaN(). The older isNaN() converts first and says true for any text, which is rarely what you meant.

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is where the last eight days start paying.
1) The data
2) Totals
reduce takes a running value and each item, and gives back the new running value. The 0 at the end is where it starts. Forget that 0 and the first turn gets an object instead of a number.
3) Filtering and sorting
b.price - a.price sorts highest first. Swap them for lowest first. The [...sales] copies the array, because sort changes the original.
4) Chaining
Note the brackets around ({ item: ... }). Without them JavaScript reads the curly brace as the start of a function body rather than an object, and you get undefined. This catches everybody once.
5) Grouping
(totals[o.city] || 0) + o.amount is the whole trick: start at zero if this city is new, add to it otherwise. One line instead of an if.
